# task-e1b6647f recurrence note

## Observed task form
Input grids can contain two sparse vertical marker columns (colors 2 and 4) and a full horizontal separator row of color 5. Demonstration outputs are uniform 2×2 grids, either all 2 or all 4. Do not assume the output color is always the more frequent marker or simply the marker with the longest vertical run; observed demonstrations do not support a reliable simple rule from these cases alone.

## Evidence from one completed instance
- Demo 1 input: 9×9, separator at row 4 (0-indexed). Above it: color 2 at (row 0, col 2), color 4 at (rows 0–1, col 6). Below it: color 2 at rows 5–6, col 2; color 4 at rows 5–8, col 6. Output was `[[4,4],[4,4]]`.
- Demo 2 input: same upper half and separator, but below it both columns 2 and 6 are present on every row 5–8. Output was `[[2,2],[2,2]]`.
- Test input: 11×9, separator at row 5. Above: color 2 at rows 0–2, col 2; color 4 at rows 0–1, col 6. Below: both columns at rows 6–9. The accepted output was `[[4,4],[4,4]]`.
- A submission of all 2s for this test was incorrect; all 4s was correct.

## Inference and caution
The output is a 2×2 uniform color, but the selector depends on a pattern feature not conclusively isolated in the available examples. In particular, Demo 2's balanced lower pair produced 2, while the visually similar test's balanced lower pair produced 4. Compare the full geometry and separator position/extent when this task recurs, rather than matching only one half or counting cells. If the recurrence gives another example, analyze what structural cue distinguishes the 2-versus-4 outcomes before submitting. Retain uncertainty; do not promote an unverified rule to certainty."
